causal.assumptions_right: The cross had room to fall from 1.25 without a fresh relative-rate shock interrupting the window, and a defined extreme plus a hard invalidation was the right expression.
causal.assumptions_wrong_or_underweighted: How little residual would remain once 1.23 traded was underweighted, as was the chance that a firm commodity tape would make any add-on a different trade from the original extreme.
causal.causal_divergence: Price and the short thesis agreed: the cross fell and the invalidations did not hit. The only gap versus a larger target is the small slip from the 1.23 exit to 1.2285, which is not a new signal.
causal.future_implication: Keep the extreme-and-invalidate framework and the habit of closing once the cross has fallen. Do not recycle this short at 1.2285.
causal.observed_reality: From 3 November to 11 November the cross fell from 1.25 to 1.23 and the short was closed after that fall. It now sits at 1.2285 on a failed 20-day floor, with Brent at 92.76 and other desks closing small shorts.
causal.original_belief: AUDNZD at 1.25 was extended and would fall unless it held through 1.255, Australian implied tightening repriced the Aussie up versus the kiwi, or a one-way commodity shock arrived.
causal.same_information_counterfactual: On the 3 November information, the short at 1.25 with invalidation through 1.255 was still the position to hold. Re-shorting after the close, once the cross had already fallen and oil was firm, would not have been the same trade.

facts.invalidation: Exit if AUDNZD holds the extreme and prints through 1.255, if Australian implied tightening keeps repricing the Aussie higher versus kiwi, or if a Hormuz shock produces a one-way commodity-FX move that prevents mean reversion.

items.future_rule: Do not re-open a closed cross short in the same swing unless price resets to a fresh extreme and the original invalidation is clearly not in force. A failed floor, peer covering, or a firm commodity tape is a reason to stay flat until a new extreme exists.
items.lesson: A cross short that has already fallen through the entry extreme is a completed expression. Re-opening it just below the exit, into a failed nearby floor while commodities are bid and other shorts are covering, treats a finished trade as a new one.
items.thesis_assessment: The belief that 1.25 was an unstable extreme was confirmed by the decline to 1.23. The close matched the preservation rule of taking the break rather than converting a finished short into a lower-entry add-on. Firm Brent at 92.76 is the commodity condition that argued against staying short even though the cross ticked a little lower after the exit.
items.what_worked: The short was opened at 1.25 on 3 November with invalidation if the cross held through 1.255, if Australian implied tightening repriced the Aussie higher versus the kiwi, or if a one-way commodity shock hit. None of those conditions printed during the hold. The cross fell and the short was closed at 1.23 on 11 November.
